chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: The chapter follows the book's own order: rectangles first, then triangles as half rectangles, then every other shape cut into rectangles and triangles. Each formula is earned by a cut and a rearrange before it is used, and each is checked on a figure the student can count.

points.title: Predict, then check
points.text: Each idea opens with a guess: which rectangle needs more powder, which triangle is bigger, will the area change when the shape slides. The video or the interactive step then checks the guess.

points.title: Cut and rearrange
points.text: Dissection is the engine of the chapter. A parallelogram, a rhombus and a trapezium are each cut and moved into a rectangle or parallelogram of the same area before any formula is written.

points.title: Height is perpendicular
points.text: Every formula uses a height that meets the base at a right angle, never a slanting side. Obtuse triangles and slanting trapeziums are handled by subtracting or adding pieces.

points.title: Tools only where the moving is the idea
points.text: Four interactive tools, each used once: stretching rectangles, sliding a triangle's top vertex, cutting a parallelogram and joining two trapeziums. Other topics are taught by worked examples.

content.text:
7.1 Rectangle and Squares
How many different ways can you divide a square into 4 parts of equal area?
One can actually think of infinitely many such ways! Consider a division, such as, and alter each part as follows.
In each part, the area is compressed along one edge and expanded along another edge. If both the compression and expansion are of the same magnitude, then all 4 parts still have the same area!
Try to think of different creative ways to divide a square into 4 parts of equal area.

content.text:
1. Predict first: how many ways can a square be cut into 4 parts of equal area? Two? Five? More?
2. Four small squares is one way. Push a notch into one edge of each part and push the same bump out of another edge: the shapes change, the areas do not.
3. Since every notch can be a different shape, there are infinitely many ways. Equal area does not mean equal shape. So what exactly is area, and how do we measure it?

What is the area of each triangle in this rectangle?
We have seen that the diagonal of a rectangle divides it into two congruent triangles. So, the area of each triangle is half the area of the rectangle.
In terms of unit squares, half the area fills exactly half the number of unit squares.
So the area of each triangle is 1/2 × 7 × 4 = 14 cm².

content.text:
Why do we count the number of unit squares to assign measures for area? Couldn't we have just used the perimeter of a region, i.e., the length of its boundary as a measure of its area?
If two regions have the same perimeter, can't we conclude that they have the same area? Or, if one region has a larger perimeter than another region, can't we conclude that it also has a larger area?
The perimeter of a region is not indicative of its area. The reason is that regions can have the same perimeter but different areas, and vice versa.
Perimeter of Region 1 > Perimeter of Region 2, but Area of Region 1 < Area of Region 2.

Worked example: Compare a 10 cm by 1 cm strip with a 5 cm by 4 cm rectangle: perimeter and area.

Answer: The strip has the larger perimeter (22 cm) but the smaller area (10 cm²)

Worked example: Compare a 4 by 4 square with a thin zigzag made of 9 unit squares joined edge to edge in one line with bends.

3. Zigzag area: 9 square units.
Answer: The zigzag has the larger perimeter (20 units against 16) but the smaller area (9 against 16)

Figure it Out (rectangles and squares, question 1): Identify the missing sidelengths. (i) A plus shaped figure is made of four rectangles: a 28 in² piece whose right edge rises 4 in above a 21 in² piece of length 7 in, a 35 in² piece of width 3 in plus the width of the 28 in² piece, and a 14 in² strip that hangs 2 in below the 35 in² piece; find the width of the 14 in² strip. (ii) A 29 m² piece and an 11 m² piece are both 4 m tall, and the bold rectangle made of the 29 m² piece and the piece below it has area 50 m²; find the missing sides.
1. (i) The 21 in² piece is 7 in long, so its height is 21 ÷ 7 = 3 in.
2. The 28 in² piece is 4 + 3 = 7 in tall, so its width is 28 ÷ 7 = 4 in.
3. The 35 in² piece is 3 + 4 = 7 in wide, so its height is 35 ÷ 7 = 5 in.
4. The 14 in² strip is 5 + 2 = 7 in tall, so its width is 14 ÷ 7 = 2 in.
5. (ii) Top widths: 29 ÷ 4 = 7.25 m and 11 ÷ 4 = 2.75 m.
6. The lower piece has area 50 − 29 = 21 m² and width 7.25 m, so its height is 21 ÷ 7.25 ≈ 2.9 m.
Answer: (i) 2 in, with 3 in, 4 in and 5 in on the way. (ii) 7.25 m and 2.75 m across the top, and a lower height of 84/29 m, about 2.9 m

Figure it Out (rectangles and squares, question 2): A path (the shaded portion) is laid around a rectangular park EFGH inside a rectangle ABCD. (i) What measurements do you need to find the area of the path? Assign values and give a formula. (ii) If the width of the path along each side is given, can you find its area? If not, what else do you need? (iii) Does the area of the path change when the outer rectangle is moved while keeping the park inside it?
1. (i) Measure the length and width of ABCD and of EFGH.
2. Area of path = area of ABCD − area of EFGH. With ABCD 20 m by 14 m and EFGH 16 m by 10 m: 20 × 14 − 16 × 10 = 280 − 160 = 120 m².
3. (ii) The widths alone are not enough; we also need the park's length and width. With a park 16 m by 10 m and widths 2 m on every side, break the path into two long strips 20 m by 2 m and two short strips 10 m by 2 m: 2 × 40 + 2 × 20 = 120 m².
4. (iii) Moving ABCD around the park changes the widths but not the two rectangles, so the path area stays the same.
Answer: (i) Path area = area of ABCD − area of EFGH (120 m² for the chosen values). (ii) Also need the park's sides; same 120 m². (iii) No, the area does not change

Figure it Out (rectangles and squares, question 3): A plot has sides 14 m and 12 m with a crosspath. What other measurements do you need to find the area of the crosspath? Assign values and give a formula.
1. We need the widths of the two paths: p for the path along the 14 m side and q for the path along the 12 m side.
2. The two strips are 14 × p and 12 × q, but they overlap in a p by q square counted twice.
3. Area = 14p + 12q − pq. With p = 1 m and q = 2 m: 14 × 1 + 12 × 2 − 1 × 2 = 14 + 24 − 2 = 36 m².
Answer: The widths of the two paths; area = 14p + 12q − pq, which is 36 m² when the widths are 1 m and 2 m

Figure it Out (rectangles and squares, question 4): Find the area of the spiral tube shown in the figure. The tube has the same width (1 unit) throughout, and its straight parts measure 20, 20, 20, 15, 15, 10, 10, 5 and 5 along the outside.
1. The hint: an L shaped tube with arms 5 and 5 has the same area as a straight tube of length 5 + 5 − 1 = 9, because the corner square is counted in both arms.
2. Add all the straight lengths: 20 + 20 + 20 + 15 + 15 + 10 + 10 + 5 + 5 = 120.
3. There are 8 bends, each counted twice, so subtract 8: 120 − 8 = 112.
4. The straightened tube is 112 units long and 1 unit wide: 112 × 1 = 112.
Answer: 112 square units

Figure it Out (rectangles and squares, question 5): A square is divided into regions 1, 2 and 3. If the sidelength of the square is doubled, what is the increase in the areas of the regions 1, 2 and 3? Give reasons.
1. Doubling the side doubles every length in the figure, both across and up.
2. Each region's area is multiplied by 2 × 2 = 4.
3. So each region grows by 4 − 1 = 3 times its old area.
Answer: Each region becomes 4 times as big, an increase of 3 times its original area

Figure it Out (rectangles and squares, question 6): Divide a square into 4 parts by drawing two perpendicular lines inside the square, then rearrange the pieces to get a larger square with a hole inside.
1. Draw two perpendicular lines through the square that are not parallel to its sides; the 4 pieces are congruent.
2. Turn the pieces so that each right angle points outward and the long edges run round the outside.
3. The outside forms a bigger square; the gap in the middle is a small square hole.
4. The area of the big square minus the hole equals the area of the original square.
Answer: The 4 congruent pieces form a larger square around a square hole; total area is unchanged

Students find missing sides from areas, find path and tube areas by splitting into rectangles, and predict how area grows when every side of a square is doubled.

content.text:
To find the area of a triangle, what measurements do we need?
We need the sidelengths of the outer rectangle.
How do we get the outer rectangle from the given triangle?
BCDE is a rectangle (how?). Let us take its sidelengths to be height and base. Then, Area (ΔABC) = 1/2 × base × height.
Since BXAE is a rectangle (how?), the height of the rectangle is the same as the height of the triangle.
Thus, if the height and the base of a triangle are known, we can find its area.
Area of a triangle = 1/2 × base × height.

content.text:
Will this formula hold for the kind of triangle, around which we cannot draw a rectangle with BC as the base?
Here is one way to look at it. The area of ΔABC is the difference of the areas of ΔADC and ΔADB, each of which can be enclosed in a rectangle.
Area (ΔABC) = 1/2 × h × DC − 1/2 × h × DB = 1/2 × h (DC − DB) = 1/2 × h × BC.
Thus, the area formula holds for all types of triangles.

Figure it Out (triangles, question 4): [Śulba-Sūtras] Give a method to transform a rectangle into a triangle of equal area.
1. Take rectangle ABCD with base AB and height BC.
2. Extend AB to E so that BE = AB. Then AE is twice the base.

content.text:
Find BY.
BY can be found using the formula for the area of a triangle.
What is Area (ΔABC)?
Area (ΔABC) = 1/2 × AX × BC = 15/2 sq. units.
The area of the triangle can also be written as Area (ΔABC) = 1/2 × BY × AC = 1/2 × 4 × BY = 2 BY.
Thus, 2 BY = 15/2. So, BY = 15/4 = 3.75 units.

Worked example: In ΔABC, AX = 3 is the height to BC = 5, and AC = 4. Find the height BY to AC.

concepts.concept_name: Diagonals and medians split area equally

content.text:
Are the 4 triangles obtained by drawing the diagonals of a rectangle (regions 1 to 4 in the figure) of equal areas?
Clearly, the triangles 1 to 4 are not four congruent triangles.
If OD and OB are taken as the bases, then we see that both triangles have the same altitude! We also have OB = OD, since the diagonals of a rectangle bisect each other. So, the triangles 1 and 2 have equal areas.
In a triangle, the line joining a vertex to the midpoint of its opposite side divides the triangle into two triangles of equal areas.

content.text:
Worked example: The diagonals of an 8 cm by 6 cm rectangle meet at O. Find the area of each of the four triangles.
1. The rectangle has area 8 × 6 = 48 cm².
2. Adjacent triangles have equal halves of a diagonal as bases and the same height, so equal areas.
3. All four are equal: 48 ÷ 4 = 12 cm².
Answer: Each triangle is 12 cm², even though they are not congruent

Worked example: BC = 6 cm and line l is parallel to BC, 4 cm away. Find the area of a triangle on BC with its top on l, and say how it changes as the top moves.
1. Base = 6 cm, height = 4 cm for every position of the top.
2. Area = 1/2 × 6 × 4 = 12 cm².
3. Moving the top changes the slanting sides, not the height.
Answer: Always 12 cm²: equal areas; only the perimeter changes

Intuition might suggest that the triangle with the minimum perimeter can be obtained by constructing the perpendicular bisector of BC. But how do we justify that this triangle has the least perimeter among all the triangles?
Let us imagine the line l as a mirror.
What can we say about the lengths of AB and its reflection AB′? Since ΔAXB ≅ ΔAXB′, AB = AB′.
So, finding point A that gives the shortest possible path B → A → C is the same as finding a point A that gives the shortest possible path B → A → C′. Choose A on the straight line BC′.
Analyse whether A lies on the perpendicular bisector of BC.

Worked example: B and C are 3 cm below line l and BC = 8 cm. Find the smallest possible value of AB + AC with A on l.

Answer: The smallest AB + AC is 10 cm, with A on the perpendicular bisector of BC

content.text:
Figure it Out (triangles, question 6): ABCD, BCEF and BFGH are identical squares, with H directly above B. The red region is the triangle DCH and the blue region is the part of square ABCD to the left of the line DH. (i) If the area of the red region is 49 sq. units, what is the area of the blue region? (ii) In another version, if the blue and red regions together are 180 sq. units, what is the area of each square?
1. Let each square have side s. Red: base DC = s, height CH = 2s, so area 1/2 × s × 2s, which is s².
2. DH rises 2s over a run of s, so it crosses AB at its midpoint: the blue triangle has legs s and s/2, area one quarter of s².
3. (i) s² = 49, so blue = 49 ÷ 4 = 12.25 sq. units.
4. (ii) Blue + red is five quarters of s², so s² = 180 × 4 ÷ 5 = 144 sq. units.
Answer: (i) 12.25 sq. units (ii) 144 sq. units

(ii) In another version, if the blue and red regions together are 180 sq. units, what is the area of each square?
1. Let each square have side s. Red: base DC = s, height CH = 2s, so area 1/2 × s × 2s, which is s².
2. DH rises 2s over a run of s, so it crosses AB at its midpoint: the blue triangle has legs s and s/2, area one quarter of s².
3. (i) s² = 49, so blue = 49 ÷ 4 = 12.25 sq. units.
4. (ii) Blue + red is five quarters of s², so s² = 180 × 4 ÷ 5 = 144 sq. units.
Answer: (i) 12.25 sq. units (ii) 144 sq. units

video_script.why: The child sees that the four triangles made by the diagonals have equal areas because neighbours share a height and have equal bases, so each is a quarter of the rectangle.
video_script.substitution: an 8 cm by 6 cm rectangle with its two diagonals meeting at O
video_script.anchor: the book's rectangle ABCD with its two diagonals meeting at O, cutting it into four triangles
video_script.wrong_answer: the triangles on the long sides are bigger
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko thinks the triangles standing on the long sides are bigger because they look wider. They are wider but shorter, and the two effects balance exactly.
video_script.payoff_line: Each triangle is twelve square centimetres
hold_back: 12 cm²
maths_rules: area of the rectangle = 8 × 6 = 48 cm²
OB = OD, because the diagonals of a rectangle cut each other in half
triangles AOB and AOD have bases OB and OD on the diagonal BD and the same height from A, so their areas are equal; the same holds for every pair of neighbours, so all four are equal
each triangle = 48 ÷ 4 = 12 cm²
check: the triangle on the side 8 has height 6 ÷ 2 = 3, so 1/2 × 8 × 3 = 12; the triangle on the side 6 has height 8 ÷ 2 = 4, so 1/2 × 6 × 4 = 12
the four triangles are not all congruent: two have base 8 and height 3, two have base 6 and height 4
video_script.design: One rectangle with its diagonals all video. Neighbouring triangles are compared by base and height, then the rectangle is shared into four. Keeko's doubt: wider means bigger.
